source_text: Patiantur ergo pueruli de istis verborum contrarietatibus quaestionem, ut nullius maioris rei quam sonorum capaces pro alludentibus sibi poculis praelientur; catholica vero fides neque iurgare adversum se legem Dei credit, neque ullam auctoritatem in exitium rationis admittit; nec cuiquam opinioni atque adulationi in maculam divinae aequitatis auscultat; sed ut Deum non solum credit, verum etiam novit omnium naturarum Creatorem; ibi peccatum nulli alii quam liberae imputat voluntati; per quae omnia traducem peccati falsam esse non dubitat.
pass_a_gloss: Let the little boys therefore suffer a question from these contrarieties of words, so that capable of no greater thing than of sounds they may fight for cups playing with them; but the catholic faith neither believes the law of God to quarrel against itself, nor admits any authority into the destruction of reason; nor listens to any opinion and flattery into a stain of divine equity; but as it not only believes but even knows God the Creator of all natures; there it imputes sin to none other than a free will; through all which it does not doubt that the tradux of sin is false.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: Let little children wrestle with a question arising from these contradictions of words, and, capable of nothing greater than sounds, fight over the cups that amuse them. The catholic faith does not believe God’s law quarrels with itself, nor does it admit any authority that destroys reason. It listens to no opinion or flattery that stains divine fairness. Rather, it not only believes but knows God to be creator of all natures; it imputes sin to nothing other than free will. Through all these things it has no doubt that the inheritance of sin is false.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
